candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — safe medication administration, adverse effects, interactions and teaching
candidate.educational_objective: Apply the cited evidence to recognize the uniquely safest or most accurate nursing response in the clinical situation tested by V2-Q0107.

options.A: Administer the medication because fetal dental effects are limited to first-trimester exposure and the client is already beyond that period.
options.B: Clarify the prescription only if treatment is expected to exceed 21 days because repeated short courses do not affect developing teeth or skeletal tissue.
options.C: Give the tetracycline with a calcium-containing meal because binding the drug in the intestine prevents clinically important fetal exposure during pregnancy.
options.D: Clarify the prescription before administration because tetracycline-class use during the last half of pregnancy can permanently discolor developing teeth.

candidate.rationale: Tetracycline-class labeling warns that use during tooth development, including the last half of pregnancy, can cause permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia. At 24 weeks, the nurse should clarify the prescription before administration rather than assume later pregnancy eliminates this risk.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Tetracycline-class use during tooth development, including the last half of pregnancy, can cause permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia.
candidate.source_locator: Tetracycline Hydrochloride label — WARNINGS: Tooth Development (last half of pregnancy; permanent tooth discoloration; enamel hypoplasia)
candidate.source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine; FDA-approved labeling)
candidate.stem: A client who is 24 weeks pregnant receives a new prescription for oral tetracycline. Which action is most appropriate before the first dose?
